---
title: "Missingness patterns"
---

The Tanaka corpus provides a useful first case because its absences arise inside a linguistic analysis pipeline, not from an invented table. In the Redwoods-style workflow described by [Tanaka et al. (2005)](https://aclanthology.org/P05-1041/), the Jacy grammar generates analyses for a Japanese sentence and a human annotator selects among them using discriminants. [Bond, Kuribayashi, and Hashimoto (2008)](https://www.anlp.jp/proceedings/annual_meeting/2008/pdf_dir/PC1-7.pdf) describe the Tanaka annotation cycle. A selected analysis carries a grammar-derived [Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS)](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~aac10/papers/mrs.pdf) representation; its predicates and links are thus not separate hand annotations.

We use the current profile extract from the [official Jacy documentation](https://delph-in.github.io/docs/grammars/JacyHinoki/) and the [pinned Jacy release](https://github.com/delph-in/jacy/tree/82c282e2592841478d07aa81a83489344bb16e00). The row unit is one sentence in one `[incr tsdb()]` profile. This release is later than the annotation stage reported in the 2008 paper, so the empirical counts below describe the pinned release rather than reproducing the paper's table.

## Loading and checking the profile table

```{r}
#| label: load-jacy-patterns
#| message: false
#| warning: false

jacy <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/jacy-mrs/tanaka-selection.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)

item_key <- paste(jacy$profile, jacy$item_id, sep = "::")

stopifnot(
  nrow(jacy) == 15000L,
  !anyDuplicated(item_key),
  sum(jacy$preferred_analysis_count) == 9128L,
  sum(jacy$preferred_analysis_count > 0L) == 8670L,
  sum(jacy$parse_readings == -1L) == 318L
)
```

The table has `r format(nrow(jacy), big.mark = ",")` items and `r format(sum(jacy$preferred_analysis_count), big.mark = ",")` preference records. Those are different units: `r sum(jacy$preferred_analysis_count > 1L)` items have more than one accepted result. Thus the selected-item count is `r format(sum(jacy$preferred_analysis_count > 0L), big.mark = ",")`, not the number of preference records.

## From a binary indicator to three observed states

Let $Y_i$ denote a downstream quantity calculated from the selected MRS for item $i$. Its availability indicator is

$$
R_i=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if at least one analysis was selected},\\
0 & \text{if no analysis was selected}.
\end{cases}
$$

The binary indicator records whether $Y_i$ is available, but it merges two observed pipeline outcomes. Some unselected items have positive parse readings, while others have no positive reading recorded. We therefore define a three-state categorical variable:

$$
C_i=
\begin{cases}
\text{selected analysis} & \text{if a preference record exists},\\
\text{parsed, unselected} & \text{if positive readings exist but none was selected},\\
\text{no positive reading} & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The release uses `-1` as a parser sentinel. It is not minus one analysis and should not enter an arithmetic count. The following recoding tests the positive-reading condition instead.

```{r}
#| label: recode-jacy-patterns

jacy$selected <- jacy$preferred_analysis_count > 0L
jacy$analysis_state <- ifelse(
  jacy$selected,
  "Selected analysis",
  ifelse(
    jacy$parse_readings > 0L,
    "Parsed, unselected",
    "No positive reading"
  )
)
jacy$analysis_state <- factor(
  jacy$analysis_state,
  levels = c(
    "Selected analysis",
    "Parsed, unselected",
    "No positive reading"
  )
)

state_counts <- as.data.frame(table(jacy$analysis_state))
names(state_counts) <- c("analysis_state", "items")
state_counts$proportion <- state_counts$items / nrow(jacy)

stopifnot(
  state_counts$items[state_counts$analysis_state ==
    "Selected analysis"] == 8670L,
  state_counts$items[state_counts$analysis_state ==
    "Parsed, unselected"] == 3666L,
  state_counts$items[state_counts$analysis_state ==
    "No positive reading"] == 2664L,
  all(jacy$analysis_state[jacy$parse_readings == -1L] ==
    "No positive reading")
)

state_counts
```

The `r format(state_counts$items[1], big.mark = ",")` selected items account for `r scales::percent(state_counts$proportion[1], accuracy = 0.1)` of the release. Another `r format(state_counts$items[2], big.mark = ",")` items were parsed but have no accepted preference record, and `r format(state_counts$items[3], big.mark = ",")` have no positive reading. Thus a zero in $R_i$ does not identify one kind of failure.

## The pattern varies across profiles

The same states can be summarized within each profile. This plot shows the observed composition directly; it does not attach a causal explanation to the differences.

```{r}
#| label: plot-jacy-patterns
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.2

profile_pattern <- as.data.frame(
  table(jacy$profile, jacy$analysis_state)
)
names(profile_pattern) <- c("profile", "analysis_state", "items")
profile_pattern$proportion <- with(
  profile_pattern,
  items / ave(items, profile, FUN = sum)
)

stopifnot(all(rowSums(
  xtabs(proportion ~ profile + analysis_state, profile_pattern)
) > 0.999999))

ggplot2::ggplot(
  profile_pattern,
  ggplot2::aes(profile, proportion, fill = analysis_state)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.78) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#2B6F8A", "#9E9E9E", "#D1D1D1") # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Jacy profile",
    y = "Proportion of profile items",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

The three-state variable locates where a selected grammar analysis is and is not available. It does not show that an unselected sentence lacks a meaning, is ungrammatical, or is rare in Japanese usage. The three states do not identify why selection failed: the grammar may not span the sentence, available analyses may be rejected, or another stage may intervene.

## A pattern does not identify its mechanism

A missingness pattern is observed data. A missingness mechanism is an assumption about the process that produced it. The profile differences above may challenge a description in which selected analyses are equally available everywhere, but they cannot establish why selection varies.

This boundary matters for downstream MRS analyses. Restricting attention to selected items changes the analyzed population to sentences for which this grammar-and-selection pipeline supplied an accepted analysis. That population may be appropriate for a narrowly stated grammar evaluation. It is not automatically a sample of all Japanese sentences.

## Inspecting the pattern

1. Why are `preferred_analysis_count` and the number of selected items different units?
2. What information is lost when the three analysis states are collapsed to $R_i$?
3. Why must `parse_readings = -1` be treated as a sentinel rather than a count?
4. Which claims about Japanese sentences remain unsupported by the profile plot?

A selected-analysis indicator represents availability, while the three-state variable retains the observed distinction between parsing and selection outcomes. Neither object identifies its own cause. The [next page](missingness-mechanisms.qmd) asks what the association with observed profile length can and cannot establish.
